messages.text:
Hello my Thor P2 arrived it’s running Thor OS out of the box with someone
else's BTC address (····) already
set as the stratum user on both pools. Is that a factory test address?
Also, the listing shows Harlo OS as installed on helium deploy.  Should it
have come pre-installed, or is it something I install myself? Thanks
Used the heliumdeploy-ops-knowledge skill
Read harlolabs.com
Searched the web · Harlo OS harlolabs latest version Hammer Thor P2
Searched the web · Hammer Thor P2 default stratum user factory test bitcoin add

Hi Jack,

Good questions, and the address one first because it matters most.

That ····... entry is not yours and it should not stay there. Hammer units are bench tested at the factory and the test rig's payout address and worker suffix are often left in the pool fields when the unit is boxed. It is not a HeliumDeploy address and nothing is wrong with the hardware, but as long as it sits in the stratum user field every accepted share is credited to whoever owns it, not to you. So change it before you let the unit run.

To do that, open the miner's web interface in a browser using the IP shown on the unit's screen (if it is not on the screen, your router's client list will show it as the newest device). Go to the pool or settings page, and in the Stratum User field for Pool 1 replace the whole entry with your own BTC address, adding a dot and a worker name if you like, for example yourbtcaddress.thor1. Do exactly the same for Pool 2, since both slots carry that test entry and the unit will fail over to Pool 2 on its own. The stratum password field can be left as x or anything the pool asks for. Save, then reboot the miner, and after ten or fifteen minutes check your pool's dashboard for your own address: you should see the worker online with accepted shares and a rising hashrate. Anything mined before the change is gone to that address, but at 10 TH/s over a few minutes it is statistically nothing, so no real loss.

On Harlo OS, here is the honest version. Harlo OS is our own firmware and it is free for every miner we sell, whatever the brand on the case, which is what the listing is telling you. It comes pre-flashed only on Harlo's own hardware, like the B30. Your Thor P2 ships with Hammer's own Thor OS, so on your unit Harlo OS is a free upgrade you flash yourself, not something already installed. It takes about two minutes: open harlolabs.com in Chrome or Edge, pick the Thor P2 model in the browser flasher, and follow the prompts. The release notes and setup guides are on the same site.

One practical tip on the order of the two jobs. Flashing replaces the firmware and clears the existing configuration, so if you intend to move to Harlo OS anyway, flash first and then enter your own BTC address once in the Harlo pool settings rather than typing it twice. If you would rather stay on Thor OS for now, that is fine too, just fix both pool fields today.

If anything looks odd after the flash, or the pool does not show your worker, the fastest help is our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf where you can tag @nullhashrate (JD, who builds Harlo OS). Reply here as well and I will pick it up.

Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support
Okay sounds good thank you!

Hi Jack,

Happy to help, and enjoy the Thor P2.

Just one last thing worth keeping in mind once you have your own address in both pool slots. Give the pool dashboard fifteen minutes or so before judging anything, since the hashrate it reports is an average built from shares and it reads low until enough shares have landed. The number on the miner's own screen will settle much faster. For a 10 TH/s unit the two should line up reasonably well once an hour has passed.

If anything looks off after that, reply here with what the screen shows and I will pick it up. The Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf is the fastest route too, tag @nullhashrate (JD) there.

Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support

Hi Jack,

On the hashrate, the Thor P2 is rated at 10 TH/s in its normal mode, and in practice most units sit a bit above that.
One owner reports a consistent 11.5 to 12 TH/s straight out of the box with no tuning
, so anything in the 10 to 12 range on a settled average is a healthy unit. Judge it on the pool's one hour or twenty four hour figure rather than the instant number, which jumps around by design.

Worth knowing before you touch anything:
the unit is rated at 10 TH/s, and running it above that, including any turbo or boost mode, counts as overclocking, which runs hotter, needs good airflow and voids the warranty
. Turning it down is the safe direction, and a lot of owners do that overnight for less power and less noise.

On the exact frequency and core voltage behind the normal preset, I am not going to quote you numbers I cannot verify, because they differ slightly between firmware builds and batches and a wrong pair is the one thing that can destabilise a good unit. The authoritative values for your machine are on the miner itself: open the web interface and look at the settings or tuning page, where Thor OS shows the active frequency in MHz and the core voltage in mV for whichever mode is selected. Note those down before you change anything, so you always have a known good state to return to. If you move to Harlo OS later, it shows the same two fields and puts the stock values one click away if you want to undo an experiment.

I have also put the question to JD, who builds our firmware and has the stock tables for these chips, so you get the confirmed numbers rather than my estimate. He picks it up tomorrow from 10am ET and the answer comes to you right here. If you want it sooner, he is active on our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf where you can tag @nullhashrate directly.

Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support
Hey thanks for the quick response. I thought 10 th/s was overclock mode ?

Hi Jack,

Fair question, and I want to be careful not to blur the two things.

The 10 TH/s is the unit's rating, which is what Hammer sells it as and what we list it at, so it is the normal operating point and not an overclock. Where the confusion comes from is that
the listing's own wording is that the unit is rated at 10 TH/s and running it above that, including any turbo or boost mode, is overclocking
. So the line sits at the rating, not below it. Normal mode aiming at roughly 10 is stock. A mode the firmware labels turbo or boost that pushes well past it is the overclock, and that is the one that runs hot and voids the warranty.

The other reason the picture looks fuzzy is that these chips often beat their own rating out of the box.
One owner reports a steady 11.5 to 12 TH/s with no tuning at all
, which is the silicon doing better than the label rather than anyone overclocking it. So seeing above 10 on a stock unit is not a sign you are in a boost mode.

How to settle it for your actual machine: open the miner's web interface and look at the mode or tuning page. Whichever mode is selected there now is what it shipped in, and the page shows the frequency in MHz and the core voltage in mV that go with it. If the selected mode is the middle or default one, you are on stock and nothing is at risk. Write those two numbers down before you change anything, so you can always put it back.

JD still has the exact stock frequency and voltage table from my earlier question, and he picks that up tomorrow from 10am ET with the answer coming to you right here. If you want it tonight, he is usually around on our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , tag @nullhashrate.

Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support

Hi Jack,

Thanks for the screenshot, that makes it clear. I can see Thor OS on 192.168.1.218, the Set tab open on General Settings, and the Work mode dropdown expanded with three choices: Normal Mode, which is the one currently selected and highlighted, Overclock Mode, and Customize voltage/frequency. The C. Voltage field below it reads 202 in the 10mV units the label uses, and the Frequency box is hidden behind the open dropdown so I cannot read it from this shot. Automatic Fan Control is on, which is what you want.

To answer the actual question: Normal Mode is the stock setting and that is the one the 10 TH/s rating refers to. So around 10 TH/s on a settled average is exactly right in Normal Mode, and many units sit a little above it, with one owner reporting a steady 11.5 to 12 TH/s untouched. Overclock Mode is the next step up, above the rating, and that is the one that runs hotter and voids the warranty. Customize lets you type your own frequency and voltage, which is the same territory as soon as you go above stock values.

So you are already on the right setting and nothing needs changing. Leave Work mode on Normal, leave Automatic Fan Control on, and judge the machine on the pool's one hour or twenty four hour average rather than the number that bounces every few seconds.

For the exact stock frequency and voltage pair behind Normal Mode, JD still has that question from me and picks it up tomorrow from 10am ET, with the answer coming to you right here. If you can send one more screenshot with the dropdown closed, so the Frequency MHz box and the Core Voltage box are both readable, plus the Dash page showing the current hashrate, I can tell you straight away whether your unit is sitting where it should. JD is also on our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf most evenings if you want it tonight, tag @nullhashrate.

Hi Jack,

Both screenshots came through and they are exactly what I needed, so here is what they show.

On the Set page: Work mode Normal, Frequency 455 MHz, Core Voltage 202 in the 10mV units the field uses, which is 2020 mV, Automatic Fan Control on. On the Dash page: 6.12 TH/s live with a 6.13 average, efficiency 10.5 J/TH, 56 shares with 1 rejected for 98.25 percent accepted, Ethernet link up with Wi-Fi off, best difficulty 167.3M, and an uptime of ten minutes.

The health signs there are all good. A 98 percent acceptance rate is normal, one rejected share out of 56 is nothing, a 167.3M best difficulty means it is genuinely finding good work, and 10.5 J/TH is a strong efficiency number. On a wired connection with the fan on auto, nothing in those two pages looks faulty to me.

Now the honest part, because you have put your finger on something I was too quick about earlier. Your unit in Normal Mode is settling around 6.1 TH/s at 455 MHz, and that pairs with roughly 64 watts at the efficiency shown. The 10 TH/s the unit is sold at corresponds to around 166 watts. Those two do not reconcile unless the rated 10 TH/s is reached in Overclock Mode rather than Normal, which is the opposite of what I told you on Monday. I am not going to paper over that: your reading of the modes looks closer to right than mine was, and I am sorry for the noise.

What I will not do is guess the stock numbers at you twice. JD builds our firmware and has the real per-mode table for these chips, and I have sent him your exact readings, the 455 MHz and 202 setting, the 6.12 TH/s and the 10.5 J/TH, so he can tell you precisely what Normal Mode should produce on a P2 and what Overclock Mode is rated for. He picks that up tomorrow from 10am ET and the answer comes to you right here.

In the meantime leave it on Normal. It is stable, cool and mining to your own address, and nothing is being lost by waiting a day. If you want the answer sooner he is usually on our Discord in the evening at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , tag @nullhashrate and paste those same two screenshots.

Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support

Hi Jack,

Thanks for running both settings for a full 24 hours. That is exactly the right way to test it, and it makes the numbers worth something.

Taking your two runs together first, because they tell us something useful. You went from 455 MHz to 500 MHz, which is about 10 percent more clock, and your average went from roughly 6.0 to 6.5 TH/s, which is also about 10 percent. That near perfect scaling is a healthy sign. A unit with a sick chip, a bad solder joint or thermal throttling does not scale cleanly like that, it flattens out or gets unstable. So whatever else is going on, your two chips are both working and responding to clock the way they should.

Against the band JD gave for Normal Mode, 6.6 to 6.8 TH/s, your 6.0 is roughly 9 percent light. That is enough to be worth looking at but not a gap that points at broken hardware. Three ordinary things produce exactly that much difference. First, a pool reported average usually reads a few percent below the miner's own figure, because rejects and variance are baked into it, so tell me which of the two the 6.0 came from. Second, chip temperature: if the unit sits in a warm spot or the intake is partly blocked, the firmware quietly trims clock to stay in range. Third, rejected shares: a steady one or two percent is fine, anything higher drags the effective number down.

So that we settle it on evidence, could you send three things after it has run a day on the stock preset again. One, a Dash screenshot showing hashrate, the average, the share count and the accepted percentage after 24 hours. Two, the temperature readings, which show on the Dash performance chart on the right hand axis. Three, roughly how warm the room is and whether the unit has clear air on all sides. With those I can tell you whether 6.0 is your unit's honest ceiling or something fixable.

One thing to be straight about on the 500 MHz run: anything above the stock preset counts as overclocking, so it runs hotter and it does void the warranty. It is your machine and plenty of owners do it, but I would keep it on the Normal preset while we work out whether it is underperforming, so that nothing muddies the comparison.

On verifying the preset itself, I have asked JD to confirm the exact stock frequency and core voltage pair that should sit behind Normal Mode on a P2, since yours reads 455 and 202, and to say whether a 6.0 average is inside his tolerance. He picks that up today from 10am ET and the answer comes to you right here. If you would rather have it sooner, he is active on our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , tag @nullhashrate and your 24 hour numbers will get a quick read there.

Hal, HeliumDeploy Technical Support
